title: Who is most at risk and where infection can come from
audience: Cleaning and support workers who enter rooms, homes or clinics where people with reduced immunity, very young children or wounds may be present.
learningOutcomes: Name four factors that leave a person less able to resist infection.
Name four sources of infection that come from outside the human body.
State who decides on extra precautions for a susceptible person.

instruction.heading: Susceptible people
instruction.body: Some people have weaker defences against infection. Very young children and newborn babies have immune systems that are still developing and have had less exposure to common organisms. Older people are often frailer, have less reserve, and rely on others for everyday tasks, which adds to the chance of injury and then infection. People living with long-term conditions such as diabetes, people undergoing cancer treatment, people with burns and people with cognitive impairment are also more susceptible. Current infection, an ongoing disease, some medicines that dampen the immune response, and several conditions at once can all lower defences.

instruction.heading: Lifestyle and environment
instruction.body: The guide lists smoking, heavy alcohol use, poor diet, lack of exercise and drug use as factors that weaken general defences. In a care setting, close contact with other people raises the risk, because more people in a shared space means more chances for organisms to pass between them. Hospitals hold more people who carry infections, so the chance of touching a contaminated surface or breathing airborne organisms is greater there. Your work is to keep the environment as clean as the schedule requires, because you cannot control the people who move through it.

instruction.heading: Sources that are not people
instruction.body: Infection can come from food that is badly cooked or past its best, and from poor hygiene around food. Water can carry organisms that are swallowed or inhaled as droplets. Soil can carry worm eggs. Waste that is poorly managed can cause infection by contact or by breathing in its fumes. Animals can transmit infection through body fluids, scratches and bites, and birds through airborne particles from plumage or droppings. Vectors such as ticks, mosquitoes, fleas and flies spread disease through bites and stings. Poor sanitation, including damp buildings and unclean surfaces, can allow fungal infection to grow. Treat any bite, scratch or sting that breaks the skin as an injury to wash and report.

instruction.heading: What this means for your work
instruction.body: Knowing who is more susceptible tells you where a lapse matters more, for example in a neonatal area or a burns unit. It does not give you authority to decide on extra precautions. That decision belongs to the nurse in charge or the infection prevention team. When extra measures are needed, carry them out discreetly. A person condition is confidential, so you must not describe it to other people in the building, and you must not move a person in a way that signals a diagnosis. Privacy and dignity apply alongside infection control.

procedure: Ask the supervisor or nurse in charge whether the area holds people who need extra care around infection. Do not ask for diagnoses.
Note any extra cleaning, waste or product requirement for that area and add it to your checklist.
Check your own hygiene and any cuts before you enter (see “Personal hygiene, clean work clothing and staying away when unwell” and “Cuts, abrasions and skin conditions at work”).
Note any non-human source you find, such as animals, pests, standing water or damp areas, and report it.
Refer any question about extra precautions to the nurse in charge or the infection prevention team.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is asked to clean a room on a children ward where an infant is being cared for in a cot.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How should the susceptibility of the infant change the way you work?
workedExamples.reasoning: Keep to the schedule, use the approved product, clean your hands before and after, and avoid contact with the cot unless your task includes it. Ask the nurse whether the cot needs any extra attention. Do not ask about the infant condition.

workedExamples.situation: A cleaner is scratched by a client cat while clearing a room in a home visit.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which step comes first, and who needs to be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: Wash the scratch using soap and water, cover it, and tell your supervisor straight away. Complete the incident record (see “Recording risks, hazard reports and breaches”). Medical advice is sought through the workplace process, and the employer decides on any further steps.

equipmentAndPpe: Disposable gloves for any task involving body fluid or contaminated surfaces
Soap, water and a waterproof dressing for any broken skin
Cleaning schedule and approved product list for the area

commonErrors.error: Assuming that only obviously sick people create a risk.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask about the susceptibility of the people in the area and plan the work to match.

commonErrors.error: Asking a client or family member about a diagnosis to decide what to clean.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask the supervisor or nurse in charge, and keep the person condition private.

commonErrors.error: Ignoring an animal, pest or damp patch because it seems minor.
commonErrors.prevention: Report it, and avoid direct contact with bites, scratches and droppings.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not attempt to judge a person immunity or medical status. That is a clinical decision.
A bite, scratch or sting that breaks the skin must be washed, covered and reported on the day it happens.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner names four factors that weaken the defences of a person against infection.
Learner names four non-human sources of infection and one control for each.
Learner states that the nurse in charge or the infection prevention team decides on extra precautions.
documentationEvidence: Record of any animal, pest, water or damp concern, with the location and the person told.
summary: Some people are at greater risk because of age, long-term conditions, wounds, current infection or medicines.
Infection can also come from food, water, soil, rubbish, animals, birds and vectors, not only from people.
Extra precautions are decided by clinical staff and carried out discreetly.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which group has the weakest defences against infection?
A worker is bitten by a dog owned by a client. What comes first?
options: Keep working and see whether it gets worse and report it if it swells
Wash the bite using soap and water, cover it and tell the supervisor
Apply a strong disinfectant directly to the skin and leave it on for an hour
Wait until the shift is over to report it and then go home

knowledgeChecks.question: Who decides whether extra precautions are needed for a susceptible person?
options: The cleaner, based on the person appearance
The client, by choosing the room
The nurse in charge or the infection prevention team
The product manufacturer, who writes the ward's own infection rules
